claims.statement: The control plane is one Cloudflare Worker script (packages/control-plane/src/index.ts, esbuild-bundled ESM) that exposes three runtime entrypoints — fetch, scheduled, queue — and re-exports the SessionDO class so the runtime can discover it.
fetch() splits on the Upgrade: websocket header before the router is reached; every other request goes to router.handleRequest with a BackgroundTasks adapter built from the ExecutionContext.

The WebSocket branch accepts only /sessions/:id/ws (regex ^/sessions/([^/]+)/ws$, else 400), returns 404 when the D1 session index has no such session, forwards the original request to the SessionDO stub, and rewraps a returned webSocket as 101 with only Access-Control-Allow-Origin.

Because the WebSocket branch bypasses router.handleRequest, upgrades get no route policy, no x-request-id/x-trace-id headers, and no http.request log line; connection admission is decided inside the DO by SessionConnectionAuthenticator.handleWebSocketUpgrade, reached through the DO dispatcher's special case for Upgrade: websocket.

scheduled() dispatches by exact string comparison on event.cron: IMAGE_BUILD_SCHEDULER_CRON ("7,37 * * * *") runs the image-build scheduler, ABANDONED_DRAFT_SWEEP_CRON ("23 * * * *") runs the abandoned-draft sweep, "* * * * *" runs the autofix queue health check plus the automation Scheduler.tick(), and any other value is logged as an unknown scheduled trigger.

The cron expressions the Worker branches on are declared outside the source, so terraform/environments/production/workers-control-plane.tf must keep cron_triggers = ["* * * * *", "7,37 * * * *", "23 * * * *"] in lock step with the exported constants; a drift silently degrades to the unknown-trigger warn branch.

The image-build cron and the draft-sweep cron are deliberately distinct and offset: draft retention is measured in hours, so riding the per-minute automation tick would cost roughly 1,440 queries a day and share its subrequest budget with automation launches.

The draft sweep archives sessions left in created for ABANDONED_DRAFT_TTL_MS (8 hours) and caps each run at 50 candidates, logging an explicit stalled-sweep error when a full batch is entirely errored.

The image-build scheduler runs its phases (recoverable-finalization republish, stale marking, provider-session cleanup, scope/branch reconciliation, artifact reaping) each in its own try/catch so one failing phase cannot abort the tick, then emits an image_build.scheduler_tick stats line.

checkAutofixQueueHealth reads only queue metrics from AUTOFIX_QUEUE / AUTOFIX_DLQ and raises autofix.queue_health errors for a non-empty DLQ, a primary backlog above 25, or an oldest message older than 5 minutes; it is scheduled via ctx.waitUntil so it cannot delay automation launches.

queue() routes between consumer batches by queue-name prefix: isAutofixQueue matches the prefix 'open-inspect-github-autofix-' rather than a substring, so an image-build finalization queue in a deployment whose name contains 'github-autofix' is not misrouted to the Autofix handler.

The control-plane worker is the configured queue consumer for both the GitHub Autofix queue and the image-build finalization queue, each with its own dead-letter queue, which is why the single queue() entrypoint must discriminate by name.

The finalization consumer applies per-message Cloudflare delivery semantics: schema-invalid jobs are acknowledged and discarded, a retry result is retried with its delay, a thrown error retries with a fixed delay, and one bad message never aborts the rest of the batch.

handleRequest builds one RequestContext per request with trace_id honoured from the incoming x-trace-id header (end-to-end correlation) and request_id always freshly generated as an 8-character slice, so per-hop identity survives while the chain stays joinable across services.

RequestContext.db is the instrumented D1 handle (instrumentD1(env.DB, metrics)) and the only database handle handlers may use; every statement's wall time plus engine meta is accumulated and spread into the single http.request wide event at the end of dispatch.

RequestContext.executionCtx is the platform-neutral BackgroundTasks capability whose submit() invokes the factory synchronously and absorbs both synchronous throws and rejections as background_task.failed, so deferred work can never fail the caller.

The router deliberately injects the raw env.DB (not the per-request instrumented wrapper) as the key for the lazy Better Auth accessors, because getUserAuthRuntime memoizes its runtime in a WeakMap on the database instance and would be rebuilt on every request otherwise.

RequestContext keeps the authorized principal separate from authentication provenance: Principal is one of user / service(+asserted actor) / sandbox, while AuthenticationContext records the browser mechanism, credential id and sig1 channel; only the router assigns a principal, and verifySandboxAuth is the single place a sandbox principal is assembled.

The router fails closed on a missing DB binding before any authentication or route matching, returning 503 Database not configured from a single honest boundary so handlers can assume ctx.db always exists without degraded-mode guards.

withCorsAndTraceHeaders wraps every router-produced response after context construction (404, 401, 403, 500, 501) with Access-Control-Allow-Origin: * plus x-request-id and x-trace-id; OPTIONS is answered before route matching with the preflight method/header set and correlation ids.

withRouteCachePolicy applies a route's declared cacheControl ('no-store' | 'private, no-store') to the response, including to authentication-failure responses, so credential-broker routes are never cacheable even when they fail.
logPrincipal emits one auth.principal event per authenticated request recording only verified identity fields (principal_kind, service, actor, user_id, session_id) and never token material.

Handler errors funnel through one mapping in dispatch: a thrown HttpError becomes error(message, status), and any other throw is logged and answered 500, so route code never plumbs Response unions through helpers.

A Route is RouteDefinition & RoutePolicy: method, anchored pattern, optional cacheControl and handler, plus authentication and supportedScmProviders. Matching filters by method and takes the first pattern match in declaration order, and parsePattern turns :name segments into anchored named capture groups.

RouteAuthentication is a closed union of public, handler-authenticated, web-service, user, user-or-service, sandbox (with getSessionId binding) and user-or-service-with-sandbox-fallback; it tells the router which authentication (if any) to perform before the handler runs, and RouteContext narrows ctx.principal per kind so handlers need no null tests.

enforceRoutePrincipal is the declared policy step after authentication: a web-service route rejects anything that is not a verified service:web principal with 401, and a user route rejects a non-user principal with 403.

For a user-authenticated route, a sig1 service:web signature is necessary but not sufficient: authenticate() must additionally resolve a Better Auth session from the forwarded headers, otherwise the request is rejected as a browser-session failure.
Sandbox policies carry a getSessionId(match) binding whose default reads match.groups.id, so a nested route such as POST /sessions/:id/children/:childId/prompt authenticates as the parent session.

Sandbox authentication is a session-runtime round-trip: the bearer token is POSTed to the DO's /internal/verify-sandbox-token path with correlation headers; a missing bearer or non-OK verification yields 401, while a thrown error yields 503 Sandbox authentication unavailable, keeping 'not authorized' distinct from 'cannot decide'.

The sandbox fallback on user-or-service-with-sandbox-fallback routes is attempted only when authentication reports failedScheme 'none'; a recognized-but-bad service signature is terminal and returns 401 without any DO call.

defineRoute merges a RoutePolicy into a route definition (policy spread last, so a route cannot override it) and performs the single cast that types ctx.principal for the handler; defineRoutes is the bulk form, and router.policy.test.ts asserts every table entry carries both policy fields.

Named policy constants (GITHUB_USER_OR_SERVICE_ROUTE, SCM_AGNOSTIC_*, GITHUB_SANDBOX_FALLBACK_ROUTE, SCM_CREDENTIALS_ROUTE, ...) are the extension point: a feature module declares handler-only route definitions and applies one policy to the whole group.

sessionRoute composes over the route model by wrapping a handler to inject ctx.sessionRuntime, the Durable Object stub client, which is how most /sessions/:id/... handlers proxy into the session while propagating trace/request ids.

supportedScmProviders gating resolves the deployment provider from env.SCM_PROVIDER (blank means github; github|bitbucket|gitlab are valid; anything else throws a permanent SourceControlProviderError), memoizes the result including the error per env value, and answers 501 for routes whose allow-list excludes the provider or 500 for invalid configuration.
Provider gating runs after authentication, so an unauthenticated request to a github-only route on a gitlab deployment receives 401 rather than revealing the deployment's provider with 501.
An invalid SCM_PROVIDER surfaces as 500 with the resolver's message even on public routes such as /health, which is the intended fail-loudly-on-broken-deployment posture rather than a degraded serve.

GitHub-only policies are the norm across the API surface; SCM-agnostic policies are the explicit escape hatch for provider-independent endpoints, and SCM_CREDENTIALS_ROUTE ([github, gitlab]) is asserted by test to be the only GitLab-listing route.

eslint.config.js bans any member access to a property named DB in production code under packages/control-plane/src (tests excluded) via no-restricted-syntax, forcing all data access through an injected SqlDatabase so reads cannot bypass dependency injection or request-path query instrumentation.

The only sanctioned env.DB reads are composition roots, each carrying an inline eslint-disable with a stated justification: router.ts (presence check, ctx.db, auth-runtime cache key), index.ts (WebSocket adapter, the three cron handlers, the Autofix queue call), image-builds/finalization-consumer.ts, and the SessionDO constructor.

The SessionDO holds a separate global-database handle read once in its constructor (nullable to preserve existing guards) which is distinct from the DO-embedded ctx.storage.sql used by session repositories.

src/env-validation.ts validates the full AES key contract rather than presence: absent, non-strict-base64 (including embedded whitespace), or a decoded length other than 32 bytes each throw, preventing both a silent AES-128/192 downgrade and a late DataError at the first secret write mid-spawn.

Env validation has no plaintext fallback and is invoked at composition time: the session runtime graph resolves both encryption keys before building any consumer, and route handlers re-validate per request before touching encrypted stores.

src/logger.ts pins service 'control-plane' on the shared structured JSON logger and exports CorrelationContext (trace_id, request_id, optional session_id/sandbox_id), the type threaded into DO- and scheduler-facing clients so ids travel as headers; the DO reconstitutes them into a request-scoped child logger rather than mutating the session logger.

Worker- and router-level loggers are constructed at module scope with the default 'info' level, so env.LOG_LEVEL only changes verbosity for loggers built inside the Scheduler, the session runtime, and the PR-lifecycle background task.

src/types.ts is the single typed contract for the Worker's bindings (DB, SESSION, REPOS_CACHE, MEDIA_BUCKET, optional service fetchers, queue bindings, per-service SERVICE_AUTH_SECRET_* keys, encryption secrets, SCM/sandbox variables), while wrangler.jsonc holds only the test binding set and Terraform owns production bindings, cron, and queue consumers.

Dispatch order in handleRequest is fixed: DB guard, context construction, OPTIONS, route match, authentication plus policy enforcement, SCM-provider gating, handler, logging, then the CORS/trace/cache wrapper — and integration tests drive worker.scheduled() with specific cron strings to prove the dispatch table itself rather than the handlers behind it.
